    Case study 02 · Coupled simulation

    FLOODABM

    A 52,141-household agent-based model coupled to catastrophe, insurance, and financial mechanics across 27 New Jersey census tracts.

    • 52,141 households
    • 27 census tracts
    • 2011–2023
    • 50 stochastic runs per scenario

    Why this problem matters

    Flood adaptation decisions change losses unevenly across households. A useful model must connect behavioral pathways to hazard, property, insurance, and out-of-pocket outcomes over time.

    How I approached it

    I designed and fielded the 937-household survey, translated pathways into agent parameters, built the household simulation, and coupled it to catastrophe and NFIP mechanics.

    What it contributes

    Coupling behavior to physical and financial feedback makes assumptions auditable and exposes where a seemingly reasonable action creates uneven consequences.

    For AI teams, FLOODABM is a stateful evaluation environment: decisions update an external system, consequences accumulate, and model assumptions remain visible.

    Research context and method

    Illustrative system architecture · not a reported study result

    1. 01Household state
    2. 02Adaptation choice
    3. 03Flood event
    4. 04Damage, payout, and out-of-pocket update
    5. 05Next annual step

    What changes in this lensOwner state includes property adaptation, insurance, damage, payout, and out-of-pocket feedback.

    Method in detail

    1. Survey-ground behavioral parameters through SEM and Bayesian calibration.
    2. Advance household adaptation and insurance decisions over annual time steps.
    3. Couple agents to flood hazard, property damage, NFIP premium/payout/deductible, and financial state.
    4. Run 50 stochastic realizations for each scenario and report aggregate distributions.

    Validation and limitations

    Validation

    • Survey-grounded behavioral parameters
    • Scenario ensembles
    • Multi-level diagnostics
    • Archived code and citation metadata

    Limitations

    • Calibration and survey evidence are place- and period-specific.
    • Household agents simplify decision processes and social context.
    • Hazard and financial outputs inherit uncertainty from coupled models.
    • Scenario results should not be treated as forecasts for an individual household.

    Evidence slice

    From question to consequence

    01Problem
    Individual adaptation choices can change long-run flood losses, insurance, and household capacity.
    02My role
    I developed and tested the household decision layer and coupled it to catastrophe-model state transitions.
    03Input
    Survey-grounded behavior, household context, flood hazard, damage, insurance, and financial state.
    04Decision
    Households evaluate protection, insurance, or no action under tenure and resource constraints.
    05Validation
    Behavioral calibration, state invariants, repeated scenarios, and comparison with public evidence.
    06Consequence
    Each annual decision changes exposure, loss, and the resources available for the next cycle.
